One Percenter Bikers: Road Rats MC (Motorcycle Club)

content.p: The Road Rats Motorcycle Club is a London outlaw biker club whose history is mostly told through its fights. It is traced to the early 1960s, when it began as a street gang before turning into a motorcycle club. Over the decades it fell out with several rivals, above all with chapters of the Hells Angels, with a club called Satans Slaves, and with another club, the Cycle Tramps. Three episodes carry most of what is known about it: a shooting during a mass fight on Chelsea Bridge around 1970 to 1971, a brawl at Cookham in Berkshire in September 1983 in which two Road Rats died, and, according to one hobby website alone, the shooting of a Cycle Tramps president in a Hastings pub in 1989.
One reference site says the club is not believed to have spread beyond London and has no chapters abroad.
content.h2: A London club that stayed independent
content.p: One biker-history website says the Road Rats of London have links back to the early 1960s, when they started as a street gang and over the years were reorganised as an outlaw motorcycle club. The same site says the Hells Angels are suggested to have once offered the Road Rats a prospect period, an offer that was turned down, and that the club remained independent. It calls this a suggestion, not an established fact.

The fullest independent description comes from Ian Richard Harris, whose 1986 University of Warwick doctoral thesis surveyed British and foreign motorcycle clubs. Harris lists "Road Rats-London" as a club founded in 1967 with one chapter, based in south and west London, with about 15 members. His list says it had earlier included Road Rats chapters at Walton-on-Thames and Richmond. He gives the colours as a brown rat on a white background with black lettering. Another site gives the patch colours as red or orange and yellow, so the descriptions do not agree.

Harris described the club as "traditionally a law unto themselves", always at war with one club or another. He also listed smaller London clubs that the Road Rats broke up. A group called Brothers-West London, with about ten members and dated 1982 to 1983, was recorded as disbanded by the Road Rats-London, and a club called Jokers-South, in south-west London, was recorded as forcibly disbanded by them.
content.h2: The 1970 to 1971 fight on Chelsea Bridge
content.p: From the early 1950s, Londonist reports, Chelsea Bridge drew motorcyclists who raced and pulled stunts across it, and it remained a Friday-night meeting point for decades. Most of those meetings were peaceful, if noisy. Londonist records that one of them, on 17 October 1970, ended in a large fight between two sets of clubs. Londonist lists the Essex Nomads and Chelsea Nomads against a bloc made up of the Road Rats, Nightingales, Windsors and Jokers. A man from the Essex side was shot and wounded, and around twenty people were arrested and spent time in prison for various offences.

The biker site names the wounded man as Peter Howson of the Essex Nomads, says he survived, and says several people were arrested, among them a Road Rats member, Paul Luttman, who it says was jailed for 12 years. That figure comes from this one source.

Harris gives a different date and a more pointed account. He dates the fight to early 1971, the point at which he says mass inter-club violence flared up. In his telling the Road Rats, an independent London club that boasted it was "better than the Angels", tried to build an opposing alliance under its own control and, when that failed, engineered the confrontation on the bridge. The brief, bloody running battle involved members of several unaligned clubs and left Peter Howson of the Hells Angels Amalgamation's Essex chapter critically injured by a shotgun wound to the stomach. Elsewhere the thesis names the wounded man "Ginger Pete" and says he was shot in the stomach. The sources therefore give 1970 (Londonist and the biker site) and 1971 (Harris, who also writes in one place that the war with the Essex chapter ran from 1970).

A 2018 Londonist feature on London biker memories adds a recollection that fits the same story. It says a man named Paterson remembers seeing a young man with his guts hanging out on Chelsea Bridge, and says the young man had been shot by a Hells Angel after his own gang, the Road Rats, declined to join the Angels. That is one man's memory, relayed by a journalist, and it does not name the victim or the date.

The aftermath, as Harris tells it, reached beyond the bridge. One club listed in his survey, Hells Angels-Cotswolds, was in his words decimated by the imprisonment of members following the shooting and disbanded two years later. He writes that after the "upheaval" the Hells Angels factions and other major clubs strengthened their territories and improved relations with one another. He writes that the Road Rats were thereafter engaged in a protracted war with all the Amalgamation chapters, plus Hells Angels England and Windsor. He records that the war with Essex ran from 1970 to 1976, with Kent from 1970 to 1976, and with Windsor from 1971 to 1980, and says the dispute with the Hells Angels clubs ended in 1976 in a peace agreement. After that, he wrote, the clubs increasingly mixed socially, though deep distrust remained and trouble was quite likely to break out again.

The Windsor chapter of the Hells Angels held a 48-hour party from Friday to Sunday in mid-September 1983 at Cookham, a village about 24 miles from London, to mark the 25th anniversary of its founding, according to UPI. The Windsor group had been regarded as renegades because they had declined to join the Hells Angels' England federation, UPI reported, and there had already been violence between the factions three years earlier. UPI called the Cookham event a "peace" or peace-making run. A participant quoted by the British press said there was "pure hate between some of these groups and they came armed to the teeth".

On the Sunday the party turned into a brawl. UPI described clans wielding chains, baseball bats, knives and axes, numbering up to 150 in all. A woman who lived nearby said the first sign of trouble was the loud rock music suddenly stopping and giving way to shrill screaming. Two men died, identified by police as Michael Harrison, 27, and Colin Hunting, 32. Their bodies were left at local hospitals, and three other victims were still in hospital in stable condition the next day. Inspector Graham Barnard said police regarded the deaths as murder, though he could not yet say what the quarrel had been about. News reports at the time named the clubs involved as Satans Slaves, from Devon in the south-west, and the Road Rats from London.

By Monday, UPI said, police had held 46 men and five women, questioned them at six police stations in the Thames valley and put 70 officers on the inquiry. The biker site says most of those present left before police arrived, and that officers recovered firearms, axes, knives, bats and lead-filled handlebars at the scene. That site says six Road Rats fought 24 Satans Slaves members. It gives the dead man's name as "Colin Bunting", where UPI prints Hunting, and gives 18 September as the date, which fits with UPI's account of Sunday. It says it is believed the fight started over women, and mentions another possible motive: that photographs had been taken of members in their colours without permission and could be used to identify them later. These are presented as beliefs, not findings.
content.h2: Who was to blame, and the 1986 view
content.p: A 1999 Guardian feature on biker feuds covers the 1983 fight in a single line, without naming Cookham. Stu Garland, editor of the magazine Back Street Heroes, is quoted saying that biker disputes can start over something as small as someone taking another man's girlfriend, and that face-saving follows once a quarrel is public. The writer adds that in 1983 it was the Road Rats against Satan's Slaves. Such fights, the piece says, are infrequent but regular, and almost invariably men die.

Harris argued that the press had the cause wrong. He wrote that the media widely linked the fight with the long feud between the Windsor chapter and the Hells Angels England federation, and called this pure speculation. In his view the deaths and many serious injuries arose from a spontaneous flare-up, "a drunken quarrel", between two unconnected clubs, the Road Rats and the Satans Slaves, neither of which had ever aspired to become Hells Angels. He said Windsor members did their best to separate the fighters and take the injured to hospital. He quoted the Daily Express writer Colin Pratt, who had claimed the meeting was a set-up by the stronger England federation to arrange a chastening showdown for troublesome rivals. Harris rejected that theory, arguing that the Hells Angels had little interest in other clubs' affairs, and that the publicity the "Battle of Cookham Wood" drew went against their interests.

Harris also argued that the scale of the response was out of proportion. Two stabbings, he wrote, were a tragedy for those concerned, but did not explain months of massive publicity. He recorded the dead as two Road Rats members, and noted that the Satans Slaves were afterwards ostracised by their former allies. He added that the Road Rats, in his survey, had lost around eight of their original and leading members in a split and that six more were then on trial, so that in his words the club's future looked uncertain. The thesis does not say what those trials were for. He also reported renewed trouble when three Road Rats were stripped of their colours by Hells Angels Holland.

The biker site gives an account of a murder in Hastings in 1989, and nothing in the other sources confirms it. In its telling, Road Rats members were drinking in the Carlisle pub, where members of the Cycle Tramps club were also drinking. After several hours without incident, it says, a Road Rats member nicknamed "Baby Rat", Patrick Boyle, began causing trouble and was spoken to by the Cycle Tramps president, Bruno "Brewer" Tessaro. Boyle left, came back with a Luger pistol and shot Tessaro behind the head, killing him. The site says Boyle was arrested and convicted of murder, and that he took his own life in prison. The site gives no date for the killing beyond the year, and no sentence. The dating is uncertain. The 1999 Guardian feature says that in 1992 the Road Rats fought the Cycle Tramps, without describing the fight, so the 1989 date rests on the biker site alone and the two sources do not clearly describe the same event.
